Brillant move. I like the async method, even if it presents a very slight increase in difficulty in workflows.

Performance AND battery efficiency is a simultaneous win-win with this async verison of API, especially with HDR pixel formats (48-bit / 16bpp via Float16)

Glad to see this coming back. 

One aspect I'm unsure about though is **the timing of the API**.
It's unclear when an author can expect the image will be available. I guess that most of the time it would be after the next paint, but I'm not sure that'd always be the case. Would it be ensured somehow that it would be ready before the next frame's painting time?
Should two simultaneous calls to `getImageDataAsync()` always resolve in a deterministic order, whatever the options?
Should any of it even be specced at all? I suppose for most use cases it's ok to be at one frame late, but having variable timings might cause issues for a bunch and might prevent the adoption of this feature.

I'd naturally expect that such an API always does that.  Generally, this is kind of "Get this image once it's unblocked", and unblocking always happens at least once per paint cycle.  

It's my understanding that getImageData blocks until the framebuffer is delivered -- so naturally I'd expect a nonblocking getImageDataAsync would report a callback right at the moment of getImageData unblock.  

However:

That being said, it would be a good idea to **explicitly mention it in the specifications**, to assauge fears of a multi-frame latency added.
Minor nit: I kinda like the `getImageDataInto()` name I came up with in #5707. For parity with `encodeInto()` from the Encoding API.
Though `encodeInto` is sync, wouldn't this create confusion somehow?

That would confusingly mean getImageDataAsyncInto() or getImageDataIntoAsync() but that becomes longwinded. The "get" prefix and "into" suffix is usually designed in APIs independently, whether you're getEncoding() or encodeInto(), rather than getEncodingInto()

Either way, I'm neutral in this case. I think @ccameron-chromium is running with the getImageDataAsync() ball.

I don't really follow the concern. We need to make sure the write happens atomically in the same task that resolves the promise. But as far as I know there's no need for a read here. Are you saying you want to enable incremental writes? As that would indeed require something along the lines you suggest, though I'm not sure why there would be a copy. Perhaps if the area to write in is a subset of the total area? I guess that's possible.

> We need to make sure the write happens atomically in the same task that resolves the promise.

Yes, exactly. This has performance implications if we don't detach the underlying `ArrayBuffer`.

If we do detach the `ArrayBuffer`, then the following implementation is possible:
* the `ArrayBuffer` is detached (no copy)
* the data from the canvas' bitmap is copied directly into the `ArrayBuffer`
  * for CPU based implementations this can happen in a worker thread
  * for GPU based implementations, this can happen using a GPU DMA engine (in theory)
* the `ArrayBuffer` is transferred back to the main thread (no copy)

If we do not detach the `ArrayBuffer`, then that isn't possible, because the write would not be atomic. Instead we would need to do
* the data from the canvas' bitmap is copied directly into a staging buffer
* during the promise resolve, while the calling thread is stalled
  * the data is copied from the staging buffer to the passed-in `ArrayBuffer`

This has two downsides. First is that we have to do an extra copy (so it is now perforce two-copy instead of one-copy). Second is that we have to stall the calling thread during that copy (which would be a real bummer if the calling thread wasn't the final consuming thread).

It seems that the design is made harder by the requirement to reuse an existing `ImageData`. How important is that? If we could do `getImageDataAsync(x, y, w, h, opts) -> Promise<ImageData>` then the issue  around detaching disappears.
 
Thinking about the implementation, the path with the least copies would involve passing a shmem fd from the renderer process to the GPU process, then doing a readback and copying into the shmem (or making the shmem visible to the GPU to readback directly. This is not always possible). So to avoid races in the case there is `ImageData` reuse, we must detach the `ArrayBuffer`.

I think the point in #5707 that this will be called at 60FPS (and ideally much more on modern displays and with spatial computing) means that we don't want to allocate all the time. I very much doubt that the allocation would be neutral.

And thinking about it some more I agree we want the semantics you outline for B, but the API shape can still be A as the `ImageData` object itself is not changing and cannot be detached. Only the backing view and buffer can be detached. So still not sure about that one I guess. I might actually lean more towards not returning the `ImageData` object since its identity can stay the same.

cc @padenot

> I think the point in [#5707](https://github.com/whatwg/html/issues/5707) that this will be called at 60FPS (and ideally much more on modern displays and with spatial computing) means that we don't want to allocate all the time. I very much doubt that the allocation would be neutral.

Some numbers here, while keeping in mind that:

1. this was on a ridiculously expensive workstation that was idle except running this benchmark on a single thread
2. DDR5 has been released since then
3. This only is regular memory copies, not GPU

https://padenot.github.io/w3c-smpte-media-production/#4

If the canvas is more or less full screen, if you have a 4k screen, say 60Hz, and we're talking rgb (and not yuv420, so one pixel is 3 bytes not 2, not even talking about higher bit depth), you barely have the budget for **one** copy, and this means saturating your memory bus anyway so everything else on the device feels sluggish. To @annevk's point, allocating new memory more or less means we fall into the cold CPU caches case here.

Obviously, not all canvas are full-ish screen, CPU caches sizes mean that there is lots of non-linearity in the copy size vs. duration, but I think it is important to keep those ballpark numbers in perspective.

I'm sure people in this thread can run some numbers for the GPU-to-CPU case, but I wanted to stress that large memory copies are important to not do, and allocations are to be minimized. The memory bus is a shared medium, you can't multi-thread your way out of this situation, CPU caches are small and finite, and the memory bandwidth can only improve so much.

Detaching/returning async can work, it can prevents TOCTOU issues. This was proposed but is not implemented yet in Web Codecs. It allows allocating a small number of canvas-sized arrays that authors can rotate.

> [#5707](https://github.com/whatwg/html/issues/5707)
> 
> I might actually lean more towards not returning the `ImageData` object since its identity can stay the same.

Thanks for the link! That's an interesting proposal.

I'm just not sure that it's possible to keep the identity of the `ImageData` object as the same. The reasons are:
Reason 1: From what I can tell, for an `ArrayBuffer`, "detached is forever". It's not possible to "deatch" and then "reattach".
Reason 2: The `data` attribute of `ImageBuffer` is readonly and cannot be changed.

I don't think it's a good idea to change the "Reason 2" part. I'm totally naive about "Reason 1". If it were possible to "re-attach", that would be best.

Assuming reattachment isn't an option, my inclination is towards
```js
   Promise<ImageData> getImageDataAsync(x, y, w, h, ImageData);
```
or alternatively
```js
   Promise<ImageData> getImageDataAsync(x, y, w, h, optional ImageDataSettings, optional ArrayBuffer);
```

In the second case, the specified `ArrayBuffer`, if specified, would be detached.
Reason 2 is false. IDL readonly is just the public API. We can totally change the value of the member. We only have to guarantee `imageData.data === imageData.data` and that we can do.

> And thinking about it some more I agree we want the semantics you outline for B, but the API shape can still be A as the `ImageData` object itself is not changing and cannot be detached. Only the backing view and buffer can be detached.

This is the same as in Streams: the Uint8Arrays, etc. cannot be detached, but their backing ArrayBuffer can be detached. I think API shape B is more consistent with the platform.
Do you remember why we decided to reallocate a view? And note that `ImageData` is a bit more than a view, it also holds some other data.

Views, at least, cannot have their backing buffer changed. ImageData can't today, but I admit that since we control it instead of TC39, we could change that. I think some code might find that breaking that invariant is unexpected, though.
The "new `ImageData object` option matches with the behavior of transferring an `ImageData` with its buffer from one context to another, this seems like the less surprising for me.

I think @padenot should at least weigh in on https://github.com/whatwg/html/issues/10855#issuecomment-2686924006. I will also double check with colleagues.

I think there is one other question here that's still outstanding from my point of view: the name. I think something like `imageDataInto()` would be a better match with existing output parameter APIs.

Regarding this proposed API, I have discovered a potential issue that might need commentary/discussion/thinking, hopefully minor (vetting for resolvable weak links or overlooked implementor notes):

# Known Performance Consideration of Overlay Use Cases

## Aka Compositing between multiple canvas types

### Use Cases

- Common games HUD overlays (generated by Canvas2D) in games (generated by WebGL/WebGPU)
- Telemetry data overlaid on top of 3D web benchmarks
- Text overlays on future TestUFO HDR WebGPU animations
- Etc.

### Potential New Problem: Forced PCIe Transfers Between GPU-RAM and CPU-RAM

Today in RGB space it's already well optimized; there's many ways to keep it on the GPU.  We have multiple APIs at our disposal now that defacto does that.  

But very few canvas APIs are HDR/WCG upgraded as of now...  So we are backed into the corner of being forced to use getImageDataAsync potentially if we want to preserve matched non-RGB colorspaces when transferring between canvas formats, and when transferring between bitmaps and textures... 

Therefore, because of this, we just want to mention this possible consideration;

Being one of the use cases for getImageDataAsync -- since it's one of the upcoming "few possible ways" to preserve colorspace formats during compositing. 

Some will do things like HTML overlays on top of canvas, but on modern GPUs it has been much faster (higher framerates) keeping parallel text overlay canvas framebuffers of same bit format (Cached Canvas2D text overlay on top of WebGPU canvas).  Whether as text sprites or matched-resolution full screen frame buffers.  Therefore, that's why some canvas-graphics users have migrated top using Canvas2D overlays (as textures) on WebGL/WebGPU CANVAS for higher frame rates or better power efficiency, since current browsers have already optimized things in a way to stay in GPU RAM (without reaching CPU RAM).  

### Commentary of Concern

WIth the introduction of new color formats other than RGB, we suddenly have fewer APIs to preserve framebuffer colorspace formats during these situations -- and thus, we run into newly reintroduced performance considerations.

getImageDataAsync is an opportunity to think the efficiencies of keeping it on GPU versus having to do the transfer over the bus.  There's many workflows that are theoretically possible including users who do getImageData to turn a bitmap into a texture, so standard documents should mention this inefficiency of this overhead (especially with rapid-changing text on high-framerate material).  

As I add WebGL/WebGPU to TestUFO while keeping suppot for text overlays, this is the approach I've adopted, and I'm trying to carefully workflow it in a way that keeps this on GPU without transferring to RAM when converting Canvas2D bitmaps to Canvas WebGL textures (regardless of bit format).  And lots of content overlay text on 3D graphics, so necessarily have to combine various different canvas formats.  It would be ideal to avoid GPU->RAM->GPU transfers.  

Make sure you mention any caveats in your standards documents, if getImageDataAsync has limitations in this regards (e.g. mandatory bus transfers), especially if it becomes one of the few ways to get a HDR Canvas2D (text overlay) to a HDR WebGL (main graphics)...

Not a problem for shared memory situations (e.g. Apple M4 RAM is also GPU RAM) but an issue for GPU over a PCIe bus (memory transfer costs, e.g. a 4K text overlay framebuffer on a 4K 3D graphics buffer).  Many workflows for text overlays is keeping two framebuffers (a transparent Canvas2D overlay + a background WebGL/WebGPU) so techniques of turning that Canvas2D to a texture without a bus transfer -- while having access to HDR -- will be something I want to stay optimized for.     There's some pros/cons with this approach -- the nice thing is that text is cached until it's updated, and the memory mandwidth of modern GPUs is so high that this is only a tiny overhead now.  So, it's become a common approach to have a text-overlay framebuffer at the same resolution as the main framebuffer.

### Why Is This Relevant To getImageDataAsync?

A napkin-exercise question to ask -- *is getImageDataAsync is potentially going to become one of the only potential upcoming ways to pull WCG and/or HDR preservation during compositing?*  Like when overlaying text (generated by Canvas2D) onto WebGPU graphics of the same buffer format.  But, it comes with the disadvantage of what may be a mandatory memory transfer from GPU to RAM, an inefficiency that some can be unaware of.**

Make sure to consider making sure the alternate APIs other than getImageDataAsync gain stay-on-GPU abilities, and review the "Considerations" sections of specs for mixed-canvas situations, where some implementors may choose the wrong API unaware of performance caveats.  

### Behind The Scene Optimizations

If some browsers do ImageData implmentations where the image data (or even parallel copy of) may stay on GPU RAM (e.g. memory mapped implementations) for graphics performance optimization situations -- then that's an interesting route; but not all browers may implement things that way.  

(I'm currently unaware if browers engines already optimize for zero-copy data transfers during getImageData via GPU-to-RAM memory mapping.)

If this is something that is already being done by any browser implementors, then you should mention a Note To Browser Implementors that zero-copy-transfer memory mapping approaches are RECOMMENDED where possible to avoid the GPU-RAM to CPU-RAM (PCIe transfer) performance cost penalty, when people are trying to preserve color-format framebuffers between different canvases, etc).

*Keywords: "Performance Consideration", "Special Considerations", "Known Issues", "Optimization Opportunities", "Note To Browser Implementors"*

Option 2 feels much cleaner and adds less GC pressure. Option 1 could be a bit more familiar to js devs I suppose, but it doesn't feel as smooth as option 2, in which you just await, and you continue with your code, and you always use the same variable.

The important bit is that memory copies are avoided.

@mdrejhon can you open a new issue with your concerns, use-case based? This is just about adding an async read back API, from a canvas (regardless of it is hardware accelerated or not) to a buffer in regular memory.

<s>
> Option 2 feels much cleaner

I disagree here. Option 2 brings a lot of unknown related to the timing of the API which will make the specs more complex, certainly the implementations too, and which will be more error prone for users.   
For instance if running something like

```js
const p1 = ctx.getImageDataAsync(imgData);
drawSomethingElseOnContext();
const p2 = ctx.getImageDataAsync(imgData);
await p1;
```
What's in `imgData` at this point? 

If you want to avoid an internal copy, then it certainly needs to be the content from `p2`, the one from `p1` just got discarded. The user may not even notice since it got a valid object to work with, just not with the content they expected.

Option1 would throw at the second call in this case, which I believe is preferrable.
</s> *[See the 2 comments below. Turns out Option 2 would also detach sync and would also throw here]*

> and adds less GC pressure

That's true, though once again `ImageData` is supposed to be a light wrapper around the buffer.

> it doesn't feel as smooth as option 2, in which you just await, and you continue with your code, and you always use the same variable.

Even in option 2 you have to change the buffer's view from which you actually manipulate the data. (Remember that `imgData`'s `.data` is a new object). It's very frequent to hold the `Uint8ClampedArray` in its own variable, or even to use an `Uint32Array` over the buffer to access each pixel on their own. I'd argue this is even worse since authors could believe they're still manipulating the `ImageData`'s buffer while they are actually working with a detached buffer of length 0.
@Kaiido the second call would throw for Option 2 as well. The underlying view/buffer still gets detached and those objects will still be (eventually) replaced.

Oh, right, it makes sense this would get detached synchronously in this case too, somehow the "replace" design made me think this would happen during the task resolving the Promise.  
Still, I feel it would be weirder/more surprising to have the `ImageData` get only temporarily unavailable, rather than definitely, like it is for other transferables and their wrappers.

> This is not a concrete counter-proposal, rather comment expressing concerns with the proposed API and strawman proposals to consider.
> 
> Feedback for:

It's unclear exactly what you're giving feedback for. To be clear, the discussion has moved far beyond the original post; the latest two proposals under consideration are in https://github.com/whatwg/html/issues/10855#issuecomment-2686924006.

Are you giving feedback on the "new ImageData object" proposal there? But that doesn't fit, because you claim that the proposal you're giving feedback on involves a copy, whereas neither of the two proposals involve a copy.

> Re: zero copy, etc
> May return direct copy-on-write mapping of ctx back buffer attached to imageData3.data

There will not be a "zero copy" way of getting data back from the canvas back buffer (at least not with an enormous number of changes to the spec).

`ImageData` has unpremultiplied alpha, is in RGBA byte order, has no stride padding, and is on the CPU. The canvas back buffer has premultiplied alpha, often is in BGRA byte order, often has stride padding, and is often in GPU texture memory layout. 

If you're interested in creating unpremultiplied image data, that is in https://github.com/whatwg/html/issues/5365. But even that won't be enough to allow zero copy (still need to ensure a specific memory layout, which might end up causing the canvas to run slower, depending on the platform, and is likely to be extremely fragile).

If we want to have hyper-optimized paths that involve reading something back, it's probably best to introduce the full path (e.g, as exist for going directly into a texture, or into an encoder, etc).

> Re: keeping data on the GPU

This can be done with `ImageBitmap` and also with the various ways of importing canvases as textures in WebGL and WebGPU and drawing canvases onto canvases. Some of these APIs allow for no extra copies, or could be created.

> > Re: zero copy, etc
> > May return direct copy-on-write mapping of ctx back buffer attached to imageData3.data

> `ImageData` has unpremultiplied alpha, has no stride padding, and is on the CPU. The canvas back buffer has premultiplied alpha, often has stride padding, and is often in GPU texture memory layout.

IIRC typical discussion related to getImageData has also involved client-side context. This was the rationale  for willReadFrequently, a feature IIRC some organisations described as very important. Maybe we should try to expand that, support that important feature first-class in this API too..

Regardless, for GPU / GPU process type scenario there will likely be a copy less.

As explained in the concerns, the pre-allocated image data cannot likely be allocated with the assumption that it can be transferred to GPU process.
This means that the GPU download + unpremul + swizzle happens in GPU process to an engine created buffer. 

If the client has provided a buffer, the engine-created buffer must be copied to the client one. 
If the engine can choose the buffer, it can do the mapping into the result image data.
And indeed supporting getImageData bgra premultiplied sounds good, for a layman like me

I think something to the extent Kimmo suggests makes sense if `getImageData()` is to be kept around as an API for dedicated workers. That is not something I had considered, but it makes sense given other synchronous APIs we make available in dedicated workers. From that perspective you'd want some symmetry between the two APIs and not completely abandon `getImageData()`. (Although maybe the symmetry should only exist in dedicated workers. I could see not supporting new features for `getImageData()` on the "main thread" to discourage its use there.)

And then it also makes less sense to pass in the `ImageData` object to reuse as you already have a bunch of its settings through other means. Hence you would pass in a view that always gets detached and the user agent may or may not end up reusing the underlying memory immediately depending on implementation-defined heuristics.

My inclination would be to have `getImageDataAsync` accept a fully-formed `ImageData` object. This will remove any ambiguities about default parameters (see the issue in #11016). 

With respect to discussions of zero copy `ImageData` backed canvas, I would envision such an API as setting the backing of a canvas to be an `ImageData`, and would be independent of `getImageData` and friends
I don't see how that addresses the concern around parity with `getImageData()`.

> I don't see how that addresses the concern around parity with `getImageData()`.

There was a proposal to have `getImageDataAsync` take an already-allocated data, to avoid excess memory consumption. That wouldn't be parity with `getImageData`. Are we abandoning that idea now?

We already have `ImageData` constructors that take buffers. So that opens up the possibility of:
```
  let imageData = new ImageData(aUint8View1, 100, 100, {colorSpace:"srgb", data:aUint8View2});
```

My sense is that that adds more confusion and complexity to the specification than just creating a version of `getImageData` that takes an `ImageData`.

The `ImageData` constructor options could also be a subset of the `getImageData[Async]` methods. If we're always going to recreate the `ImageData` anyway I don't really see why we'd use that for the reuse memory scenario.

That seems reasonable. I'll marinate it a bit more.

If we had a time machine, then I think we'd change the APIs to be:
- specify default arguments for all `ImageDataSettings` parameters (#11016)
- add `data` as a key to `ImageDataSettings`
- not add `ImageDataSettings` parameters to the constructors that already take `data`
